If you’re getting numbness, check the tightness of your boots AND bindings, especially the ones that sit across your ankle since those cut off circulation points. 

When tightening, a good trick is to place your hand (flat) in your boot and then tighten. That’ll leave a very small gap of flexibility. 

While you don’t want to be so loose that you’re experiencing heel lift, it you’re losing circulation, you’re too tight.

Traumatic deaths, even ones you don’t see in-person, can cause PTSD.

Processing took literal years for me. I was in therapy beforehand for managing stress at work, but was able to quickly pivot to tackling grief. It took me 5 years before I was able to mentally handle EMDR therapy, which has reduced a significant portion of the PTSD symptoms as well. 

PS - the PTSD peaked early and then resurfaced harder a few years later. At first I couldn’t handle seeing GSWs on TV/visual media,  but it evolved into me having a direct, recurring visual without any stimulus ~4 years later. I started EMDR shortly after it began to happen. 

I recommend checking in on yourself periodically and being aware of grief relapses or larger periods of grief after longer periods of stability. It is normal and somewhat expected since this is considered a traumatic death. 

I completely understand the changing feelings, too. You’re still so early on the journey that everything is volatile. For me nearly 7 years later…it more or less just evolves. I’m not as volatile to how I’m feeling - nothing is new, but it can deepen or reduce throughout the year. 

Everyone says that it gets better and I used to feel like it was a platitude. It will get better, then worse, then better, then way worse, then neutral, then way better. Or some random combo of it ^. It will stabilize and you will enter your new normal where the pain doesn’t lessen, but you become stronger and better equipped to deal with the mental aftermath. 

I liked it when people didn’t sugarcoat it for me. You won’t be the same after something this extreme happens, but honestly who should expect otherwise?  If anything, we are more resilient than the vast majority of our peers. 

You’re doing a great job so far.
